CENTRAL CONTRIBUTION:
This work presents Viral.izo 2.0, an enhanced casual educational game designed to foster resource management skills against emerging viral attacks, extending a previous version by incorporating three new game levels of progressive difficulty, three distinct virus variants with unique behaviors, two novel minigames, and a local ranking system, alongside a comprehensive User Experience (UX) assessment.

PROBLEM AND CONTEXT:
The COVID-19 pandemic, characterized by its global spread to 220 countries and territories with over 186 million cases and 4 million deaths by mid-2021, highlighted the critical need for effective health awareness and promotion, especially among children and young people during lockdowns. Digital games emerged as a significant tool for entertainment and mental well-being, influencing health promotion by encouraging adherence to WHO guidelines such as social distancing and hand hygiene. While various educational games like Heroes of the Pandemic, Virus Combat, and Plague Inc: The Cure have addressed health promotion, Viral.izo 2.0 aims to offer a more engaging and comprehensive experience by focusing on strategic resource management against evolving viral threats through an updated game design and rigorous user evaluation.

METHOD/SYSTEM:
Viral.izo 2.0 was developed using the Unity game engine and C# scripting, following a methodology rooted in Software Engineering and agile practices, including remote meetings, a detailed Game Design Document (GDD), and roles like Product Owner (PO) and Scrum Master (SM). The game's narrative involves a scientist creating an antibody cloud (the player's avatar) to be sent back in time to combat a pandemic virus and its variants spreading globally (Figure 2). The player controls the antibody cloud with a mouse, with its size directly proportional to its strength; a smaller size allows faster movement and greater accuracy, leaving a visual trail (Figures 3.b, 3.c).
The game features four progressively difficult levels with unique 2D maps (Fortaleza, Ceará, Brazil, and the world map) and diverse enemies (Figure 3): an original virus (Level 1, default speed/damage), Variant 1 (Level 2, 25% faster spreading speed and increased spawns), Variant 2 (Level 3, more aggressive damage, causing antibody cloud size reduction and point loss even when defeated), and Variant 3 (Level 4, combining spread and damage behaviors of Variants 1 and 2). Bacteria are also present, causing minor damage without leading to defeat (Figure 3.e). Visual effects, including particle system-generated emissions for each virus variant (e.g., spherical black for original, circular with transparency for Variant 2, cone-shaped red for Variant 3, "doughnut" yellowish for Variant 4), enhance dynamic collisions and realism (Figure 4). Players collect various personal protection items (e.g., Simple mask, PFF2/N95, Face shield, Vaccines, Gel alcohol, Elmo, EVA, Ventilator, Ambulance) (Figure 5), which provide bonuses like increased cloud size, speed, score doubling, or extra lives (e.g., "Elmo").
Two new minigames are strategically placed between levels 2 and 3 (Minigame 1) and levels 3 and 4 (Minigame 2), triggered by a scientist character to provide health bonuses and prepare players for advancing levels (Figure 7). Minigame 1 (Figure 9) is a card-based educational game where players chronologically order 8 of 16 historical COVID-19 pandemic events (e.g., WHO alert on Dec 31, 2019; SARS-CoV-2 naming on Feb 11, 2020; Delta variant in Dec 2020; Omicron variant on Nov 24, 2021), earning 0-16 bonus points. Minigame 2 (Figure 10) is an endless runner where the player controls a "second vaccine dose" to evade viruses and their variants, with increasing camera speed over time, awarding bonus points proportional to invincibility duration. A local ranking system (Figure 8.b), implemented using serialization and JSON, records the top five scores based on collected items and antibody cloud size, saved only for completed and survived matches.

RESULTS AND METRICS:
User Experience (UX) assessment was conducted with 16 participants (aged 20-32, 15 undergraduate, 1 graduate Computer Science students from UNIFOR), utilizing the 38-question Core Elements of Gaming Experience (CEGE) questionnaire by Calvillo-Gámez et al. (2015) on a 7-point Likert scale, supplemented by two subjective questions. For positively worded items, the overall average score was A=5.68 (SD=2.0), with the highest satisfaction for "The graphics were appropriate for the type of game" (Item 26), receiving 87.5% "Strongly Agree" and 12.5% "Agree" responses. The game was generally not perceived as difficult, with "The game was difficult" (Item 35) receiving only 6% "Strongly Agree" and 6% "Agree." For negatively worded items, the average score was A=3.0 (SD=1.67), indicating low frustration, with most responses clustering in "Strongly Disagree," "Disagree," and "Somewhat Disagree" (Figures 11, 12, 13, 14). Diverging scores for items 18 ("I usually do not choose this type of game") and 19 ("I did not have a strategy to win the game") suggest that participants might not be frequent players of casual games or found the minimalist instructions insufficient. Subjective feedback included suggestions for integrating play-time and scores on the ranking screen, implementing an online multiplayer mode, and recalibrating Minigame 1 difficulty (e.g., providing two extra lives). Minigames were positively described as fast, surprising, bonus-generating, and adrenaline-inducing. Overall, the evaluation results were "very positive."

LIMITATIONS:
Minigame 1's high difficulty level was identified as a limitation, potentially hindering players' ability to learn the chronological order of pandemic events effectively. The ranking system is currently local, which limits competitiveness to a single device and does not support broader online interaction. The intentional minimalist instructions provided to participants for evaluation purposes sometimes led to initial confusion regarding gameplay mechanics.

KEY CONCEPTS:
Game-based Learning (GBL), Resource Management, User Experience (UX) Assessment, CEGE Questionnaire, Unity Game Engine, Agile Development, Local Ranking System, Minigames (Card Game, Endless Runner), Antibody Cloud, Virus Variants, Particle System.
